common_name: Lady Banks Yellow Rose (Double Yellow Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring against a large arbor, pergola, or old tree, since this is the most commonly grown, extremely vigorous form of Lady Banks rose and needs a substantial structure to climb into over the years.

directions: Plant against a large, permanent support in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous room for a mature climber that can eventually cover an entire arbor or old tree. This is the double yellow, essentially unscented form of Lady Banks rose, the one most commonly sold in Southern nurseries, prized for smothering itself in small rosette blooms in a single, spectacular spring flush and for being nearly thornless and pest-free once established. It is somewhat more cold hardy and noticeably more vigorous than the white double form, tolerating heat and drought with ease but flowering only once a year rather than repeating. Prune only right after the spring bloom finishes, since flower buds form on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's display.

common_name: Lady Banks White Rose (Fragrant Double White Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring against a strong fence, pergola, or old tree; this white-flowered form of Lady Banks rose is slightly less vigorous and cold hardy than the common yellow form, but carries a distinct violet-like fragrance.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun against a substantial, permanent support, since this heirloom climber, first brought from China in the early 1800s, eventually covers a large structure with age. Unlike the more common yellow-flowered form of Lady Banks rose, this double white selection carries a light, sweet violet fragrance and is a little more restrained in size, though still a large, thornless climber capable of scaling an old porch or tree. It flowers only once, in a heavy spring flush of small, rosette-shaped double blooms, and tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established. Prune immediately after flowering rather than in winter, since next year's blooms form on the current season's mature wood.

common_name: All the Rage Rose (Orange-Red Easy Elegance Landscape Rose)
subcategory: landscape shrub rose, Easy Elegance series

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other Easy Elegance roses this cultivar is grown on its own roots, so a winter dieback still regrows true to type.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow air movement through the dense, rounded habit. All the Rage is part of Bailey Nurseries' Easy Elegance line of own-root landscape roses, valued for vivid orange-red, semi-double blooms held in loose clusters against glossy foliage, and for strong resistance to black spot and powdery mildew without a spray program. Its compact, mounded form fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass beds, and it reblooms in flushes from late spring to frost with spent flowers dropping cleanly on their own. Being grown on its own roots rather than grafted, the plant recovers true to type even after a hard winter dieback or damage to the crown.

common_name: Nearly Wild Rose (Single Pink Landscape Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this compact, own-root shrub has been a dependable low-maintenance landscape rose since its introduction in 1941.

directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil, spacing plants close enough that mature shrubs knit together for a low informal hedge or mass planting. Nearly Wild bears simple, single, wild-rose-like pink flowers with a ring of pale gold stamens at the center, produced in such abundance and so continuously from late spring through frost that the small, rounded shrub is rarely without bloom. It is notably tough and disease resistant for an older cultivar, asking for little beyond an annual shaping in late winter and occasional watering during extended dry spells. Its modest size and reliable, nearly nonstop flowering have kept it in wide commercial production for decades as an easy-care landscape and hedging rose.

common_name: Carefree Wonder Rose (Pink Blend Landscape Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this 1990 Meilland introduction was one of the first widely marketed low-maintenance landscape roses and remains a dense, reliable performer.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing room for a dense, rounded shrub that fills in quickly. Carefree Wonder produces two-toned, semi-double blooms in bright rose pink with a creamy white reverse and a pale eye at the base of each petal, opening in generous clusters against dark, leathery foliage with notably good resistance to black spot. It repeats reliably in flushes from late spring through fall and, once established, tolerates heat and short dry spells with only moderate watering. An occasional shaping cut in late winter and light deadheading of spent clusters through the season keeps the shrub tidy and encourages the next flush.

common_name: Petite Knock Out Rose (Dwarf Compact Landscape Rose)
subcategory: landscape shrub rose, Knock Out series

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this dwarf member of the Knock Out family suits containers, small beds, and border edges where the full-size originals would outgrow the space.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, in a container, small bed, or border edge sized for its diminutive mature form. Petite Knock Out shrinks the familiar Knock Out family down to a compact 18 to 24 inch rounded mound while keeping the same single red blooms, continuous rebloom without deadheading, and outstanding resistance to black spot that made the original a landscape staple. Its small scale makes it well suited to patio containers and tight foundation plantings where a standard Knock Out would quickly overwhelm the space. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain its neat, rounded shape; otherwise it needs only routine watering and feeding through the season.
